title: Astronomers Detect First Possible Moon Outside Our Solar System
excerpt: A Jupiter-sized object orbiting a brown dwarf 71 light-years from Earth could be the first exomoon ever found, but the discovery has scientists debating whether existing cosmic labels still apply.
body:
• Astronomers have detected a possible moon-like object orbiting a brown dwarf in the CD-35 2722 star system, located about 71 light-years from Earth.
  • The object is a gaseous body with at least 90% of Jupiter's mass, completing an orbit every 170 days.
  • This discovery challenges traditional definitions of moons, as the object is larger than any known moon in our solar system and orbits a brown dwarf rather than a planet.
  • The findings were published in the journal Nature and represent a significant milestone in the search for exomoons.

Astronomers have found the strongest evidence yet for a moon-like object beyond our solar system — but the discovery is so strange that scientists aren't even sure what to call it. The object orbits a brown dwarf in the CD-35 2722 star system, roughly 71 light-years from Earth, and was detected using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile. The findings, published on July 22 in the journal Nature, mark a potential milestone in a decades-long search for exomoons.

A Three-Body System Like No Other

The CD-35 2722 system is built like a set of nesting dolls. A red dwarf star, about 40% the mass of our sun, sits at the center. Orbiting it is a brown dwarf — a celestial body too massive to be a planet but too small to sustain the nuclear fusion that powers a star — roughly 33 times heavier than Jupiter and 50% larger. And orbiting the brown dwarf is the newly detected object: a gaseous body with at least 90% of Jupiter's mass, completing one lap every 170 days at a distance about one-fifth of that between Earth and the sun.

By the logic of our own solar system, an object orbiting something that orbits a star should be called a moon. But this "moon" is bigger than any planet in our neighborhood except Jupiter itself.

"We deliberately chose not to call it a moon. That's because this object is unlike any moon in our solar system. It's much more massive, and it doesn't orbit a planet — it orbits a brown dwarf, an object that's somewhere between a planet and a star."

— Alice Zurlo, Universidad Diego Portales astrophysicist and YEMS director

How They Found It

Lead author Kevin Hoy, a doctoral student at Universidad Diego Portales and affiliated with the European Southern Observatory, used radial velocity analysis to make the detection. The technique measures tiny wobbles in a celestial body's motion caused by the gravitational tug of an unseen companion — the same method that led to the discovery of the first exoplanet around a sun-like star in 1995.

Between October 2023 and February 2026, Hoy's team monitored the brown dwarf using the VLT's CRIRES+ spectrograph. Their data revealed a repeating velocity pattern every roughly 170 days — the telltale signature of an orbiting object. A best-fit model also hinted at a second, closer satellite with about 28% of Jupiter's mass and an 87-day orbit, placing the pair near a 2:1 orbital resonance similar to the Galilean moons of Jupiter, according to the study.

What Comes Next

Hoy plans to perform astrometry analysis to measure the true mass of the exosatellite and calculate its orbital angles. His team could also apply the radial velocity technique to other brown dwarfs to see if similar objects are common or rare. The system's youth — the brown dwarf is still glowing with residual heat from its formation — offers an additional window into how such objects might form, whether from a disk of gas and dust around the brown dwarf or through gravitational capture.

"I think this discovery has opened a Pandora's box for the scientific community," Zurlo told Reuters. "This type of object is completely new and unusual, truly different from what we are familiar with in our solar system."

The search for the first confirmed exomoon is not over. But the CD-35 2722 system has given astronomers their best lead yet — and forced a reckoning with the limits of the vocabulary they built to describe their own cosmic backyard.
